sections.title: Segula Remedies, Incantations and the Ways of the Emori
sections.html:
It is forbidden to use segula remedies (remedies whose effect is unexplained) or incantations that draw on the power of idolatry, because of the prohibition of idolatry (SA YD 155:1; above 4:4). Likewise it is forbidden to use segula remedies or incantations that draw on forces of impurity and destructive angels, because of the prohibition of sorcery. Likewise it is forbidden to use segulot and incantations from gentile customs unless physicians or healers claim that they are effective, because of the prohibition of 'the ways of the Emori' ('the customs of the gentiles'). But when the segulot and incantations do not draw on forces of impurity, and in the opinion of healers they are effective, even though there is no explanation of the way in which they work and their benefit appears to be like a segula, as long as it is evident that they are intended for healing, it is permitted to use them.

For it to be evident that they are for healing, physicians or healers to whom people customarily turn must hold that they can heal. Even healers using alternative methods that have not been proven by scientific research may determine that something is a remedy, since people customarily turn to them for medical purposes. Even remedies that idol worshippers and sorcerers originally claimed worked by magical power – if healers who are not connected to that belief now estimate that they are effective and recommend them, it is permitted to use them. This is as the Sages said (Shabbat 67a): one who suffers from earache may take a locust's egg and attach it to his body to ease his pain, and one who suffers from sleep disturbances may take a fox's tooth. Even on Shabbat he may go out with them into the public domain, for since the physicians of those days held that they could be effective, they are considered part of his clothing (Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 19:13; SA OḤ 301:27).

Likewise, the Sages permitted (Shabbat 67a) the use of incantations that were known in those days to be effective. Most incantations were said together with certain segula actions. For example, one who had a bone stuck in his throat would bring another bone of the same kind, place it on his head and say: "Ḥad ḥad naḥit bela, bela naḥit ḥad ḥad" (one by one, go down, be swallowed; be swallowed, go down, one by one). And if a fish bone was stuck in his throat, he would say: "Nina'atzta ke-maḥat, nin'alta ke-tris, sheya sheya" (you are stuck in like a needle, you are locked in like a shield [?]; go down, go down [?]). All this is on condition that healers claim that they are effective. Even when there is no explanation of how they work, since in practice healers think that they are effective, it is permitted to use them. For it is possible that they work in a way that physicians do not yet understand, and perhaps they work psychologically (like the placebo effect).

But remedies and incantations that, in the opinion of healers of all kinds, are not effective, and for which there is also no explanation of how they could be effective, since they are done in imitation of the practices of the gentiles, are forbidden because of 'the ways of the Emori'.1

sections.title: Do Segula Remedies Override Prohibitions?
sections.html:
It is a well-known rule that pikuaḥ nefesh (saving life) overrides the prohibitions of the Torah, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My laws, which a person shall do and live by them; I am the Lord." The Sages expounded (Yoma 85b): "'And live by them' – and not die by them," meaning that the mitzvot of the Torah were given so that people should live by them, and not die through fulfilling them. Therefore any remedy needed to save a dangerously ill person is administered, even when it involves desecrating Shabbat or eating forbidden foods.

However, the poskim disagreed whether it is permitted to transgress Torah prohibitions for segula remedies too. For example, a person swallowed a deadly poison, and someone there knows how to write an amulet intended to induce vomiting of deadly poison, and the question is whether it is permitted to write the amulet on Shabbat (see Birkei Yosef OḤ 301:6).

Some say that segula remedies have the same law as ordinary remedies that heal by natural means, and it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat in order to heal with them. For a natural remedy too does not heal with certainty, and it is not known with certainty how it heals, and nevertheless Shabbat is desecrated to prepare it, because even a doubtful danger to life overrides Shabbat and other prohibitions (Yoma 83a). Similarly, it is permitted to desecrate Shabbat to prepare a segula remedy that might heal a dangerously ill person. And any segula remedy that the people there regard as a proven remedy that can save life – it is a mitzva to transgress Torah prohibitions in order to save the sick person by means of it. Therefore it is permitted to write on Shabbat an amulet that experience has shown is capable of saving a dangerously ill person (Rashba).

On the other hand, some say that there is nothing to segula remedies, and they were permitted only in order to set the sick person's mind at ease; for this purpose one may transgress rabbinic prohibitions, but not Torah prohibitions. Therefore it is forbidden to write an amulet on Shabbat (Rambam).

In practice, since in recent generations medical science has developed, ordinary remedies have become very well tested, whereas segula remedies are not tested; therefore one should not transgress Torah prohibitions for segula remedies.2

sections.title: Healing, Reiki and Healing Methods from the East
sections.html:
There are alternative medical methods, such as healing and Reiki, that are based on Eastern teachings such as Buddhism and Taoism. According to the healers who use these methods, by touching certain places on the body, or by placing the hand above those places without touching, they channel healing energy from the cosmic energy, and thereby give the body strength and restore its natural balance, so that it can overcome its pains and illnesses. Some healers even claim that they can send healing energy to people who are at a great distance from them. The meaning of the word 'healing' is recovery and cure, and it refers to a group of medical methods, the best known of which in Israel is Reiki, which also has various branches.

These methods are not based on systematic scientific research and are therefore not accepted by the medical establishment, and in the opinion of the overwhelming majority of physicians they have no power to bring about healing, apart from the psychological influence that can heal (the placebo effect). On the other hand, there are quite a few people, from all sectors of the population, who claim that they were relieved of their pains and illnesses by healers practising healing and Reiki.

Some say that it is forbidden for Jews to be treated by these methods, because they rest on idolatrous conceptions, for the 'cosmic energy' by means of which they heal is called by them 'the power of chi', and in these authorities' opinion it is an idolatrous power. In their opinion, the terms that the practitioners in the East used are also idolatrous, and likewise the phrases of concentration and requests for help that some healers say before treatment are an appeal to idols. They further argued that using these methods transgresses the prohibition of sorcery. In addition, according to the stringent, from a medical standpoint these methods are false, and they were founded on the idolatrous conception at their root, and consequently they are forbidden because of 'the ways of the Emori'.

But the main view is that of those who permit using these healing methods. They have no idolatrous aspect, since the power of chi is a general idea of faith about the life force found in all creatures, which involves no idolatrous corporealisation. True, there are people of the East who believe in this power as part of an idolatrous faith, but it is not necessary to connect the conception of the power of chi with the idolatrous conception. And even if these medical methods originally grew among people with an idolatrous conception, since in practice the healers do not believe in idols and the healing process involves no idolatrous worship, the rule applies to them that "anything that has a healing purpose does not involve the ways of the Emori" (Shabbat 67a). For the prohibition of 'the ways of the Emori' applies to customs that have no reason other than being an accepted tradition of foreign religions, whereas here we are dealing with things done for the sake of healing and not as a gentile tradition. There is no need for the healers who practise these remedies to present Torah scholars with proof that they are effective, because Torah scholars need not decide medical questions and examine all the research and its degree of reliability, but only consider whether those healers and their clients regard this matter as medicine or as a ritual tradition; and since it is regarded by them as medicine, there is no prohibition in it.

However, one should not permit desecrating Shabbat or eating forbidden foods in order to carry out alternative medicine, for in this matter one follows the majority of physicians or the greater experts. And it is indeed clear that physicians practising establishment medicine are the majority, and they are also considered more expert since their words rest on systematic scientific research, and they do not regard these remedies as proven remedies. However, it seems that if the sick person is convinced that his life can be saved by the alternative medicine, he may desecrate Shabbat or eat forbidden foods according to their instructions (see Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 8:4, note 5).3

sections.title: Other Alternative Remedies (One Brain, the Pendulum and Homeopathy)
sections.html:
There are many alternative methods; we will deal with three, and from them we can learn about the other methods. 'One Brain' (applied kinesiology): the healers using this method hold that a person's brain is aware, in his subconscious, of the root of the problems from which he suffers. Therefore, while the patient is asked questions, it is possible to know from the response of his muscles what is true and what is false, and thereby to locate the roots of the medical and psychological problems from which he suffers and the time at which they began to develop, and on that basis to offer him solutions and remedies.

Pendulum: the healers using this method customarily hold in their hand a string to which a stone or piece of metal is attached, and while concentrating on not moving their hand, they ask the patient questions, and understand the answers to the questions according to the movement of the pendulum. In their conception, in the depths of consciousness the practitioner can know the answer, and according to the movement of the pendulum, which is moved by an unconscious movement of his, he can decipher the illness and the way to cure it.

Those who believe in these methods describe cases of patients whose problem the ordinary medical system failed to locate, whereas healers using these methods succeeded in hitting the mark. Sometimes they send the patients for ordinary treatment in the medical system, while reinforcing the treatment with alternative remedies, and sometimes they carry out all the medical treatment that they consider necessary.

Homeopathy: this method is based on the hypothesis that the same substance that can cause a certain illness, if diluted greatly in a liquid until only a faint trace of it remains, will stimulate the body to cope with that illness and be healed.

Some hold that it is forbidden to go to healers using these methods, because according to the position of the medical establishment and the overwhelming majority of physicians, these methods have no factual basis. And all the claims of the healers using these methods that they helped patients – in the best case they helped through psychological influence (the placebo effect), and in the worst case they did not help at all and their words are falsehood and fraud. It emerges that one who goes to them abandons the mitzva to heal his body and errs in receiving sham treatments that have no benefit. In addition, following false methods distorts a person's thinking and causes him to err in understanding the Torah and its guidance. Regarding 'One Brain' and 'Pendulum', in the opinion of the stringent this also involves the Torah prohibition of 'a diviner' (kosem), which consists of divining the future and hidden things through various actions that help him sink into a meditative consciousness that will enable him to know hidden things (see above 24:1).

But as explained in the previous section, although it is very possible that there is no medical benefit in these remedies, as the medical establishment claims, there is no prohibition against trying to be healed by them. For healers using these methods need not prove scientifically that they are beneficial in order for it to be permitted to use them; it suffices that many people go to healers using them in order to be healed and not in order to perform a ritual. As the Sages said (Shabbat 67a): "Anything that has a healing purpose does not involve the ways of the Emori." Nor is it the role of halakhic scholars to fight the medical establishment's war against alternative healers. And although it is reasonable that the medical establishment is right in most of what it says, it is possible that these remedies are effective psychologically. Likewise, it is possible that despite the many successes of the medical establishment in various fields, there are many things it has not yet understood, and in the future scientific research will prove that in some matters the alternative healers were right.4

However, it is right for a person not to be enticed by unfounded rumours or passing moods, and to examine his ways with reason. But once he has reached the conclusion that alternative medicine can bring relief to his illness and his pains, there is no prohibition for him to turn to it, provided that he does not do things that, according to establishment medicine, are dangerous to his health; for in a situation of disagreement, one should act according to establishment medicine, since this is the opinion of the majority of physicians, and their opinion rests on systematic trials by the greater experts, as explained at the end of the previous section.

sections.title: Not Using the Remedies Mentioned in the Talmud
sections.html:
In a number of places in the Talmud medical recommendations are cited for curing various illnesses and ailments (Shabbat 109b-110b; Gittin 67b-70b; and elsewhere). However, in practice the poskim ruled that one should not use the remedies and incantations that were customary in the days of the Tanna'im and Amora'im and are cited in the Talmud. There are several reasons for this:

First, the remedies and incantations that the Sages cited do not express a halakhic position; rather, this was the position of the physicians in their time, and all that the Sages came to teach us is that it is a mitzva to be diligent about bodily health, and for this purpose it is also right to know the guidance of the physicians and to act according to it. But when the position of the physicians has changed, one should act in each generation according to the guidance of the physicians of that generation, whose position is based on the experience that has accumulated in their hands, from the earliest generations until their own day (Rav Sherira Gaon and his son Rav Hai Gaon).

Second, as times change nature too changes, and therefore remedies that were good in the days of the Sages are no longer good in later generations. For example, it is possible that bacteria and viruses that were widespread in the past have become less widespread, and other bacteria and viruses have become more widespread in their place, or that over the years bacteria have developed resistance to the old remedies, and therefore they are not effective today (see Tosafot, Mo'ed Katan 11a, s.v. "kavra"). Likewise, changes in dietary habits can change the effect of remedies.

Third, even if the remedies cited in the Talmud could be effective today, in practice it is impossible to carry them out precisely, because some of the names of the herbs and substances have changed, and the quantities and methods of use that were known in the past have been forgotten (Maharil, Minhagim, Likkutim 43; Ḥavot Ya'ir 234).

Fourth, since it has become clear that there is a reasonable chance that the remedies mentioned in the Talmud will not be effective, there is a concern that if people try to use them and it is found that they were not effective, they will mock the words of the Sages (Maharil). Therefore the early authorities issued a ban, "that one should not rely on the remedies of the Talmud" (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 8:12). From this standpoint the prohibition applies specifically to the remedies and incantations written in the Talmud, but it is permitted to use other remedies and incantations that have been handed down by tradition from ancient times, and that healers claim might perhaps be effective as a remedy. And although these remedies are no better, since they are not cited in the Talmud, there is no concern that if using them is not effective, people will mock the words of the Sages because of them.5

sections.title: The Prohibition of Turning to Sorcerers on Behalf of a Sick Person
sections.html:
Sometimes a relative is sick with a severe and terminal illness that, according to the physicians, has no cure, but the family members, worried about their loved one, are not prepared to accept the decree, and try to find remedies with sorcerers, who claim that by means of magical actions they will succeed in healing the sick person. The poskim disagreed on the question whether it is permitted to turn to a non-Jew who engages in sorcery on behalf of a sick person.

Some permit it, because in their opinion there is no prohibition for a gentile to engage in sorcery. True, as a rule it is forbidden for a Jew to make use of non-Jewish sorcerers, because of the positive mitzva of "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" (Devarim 18:13), by which we are commanded to accept God's governance and not to try to change it by unnatural means (above 19:12-13). But when it concerns a sick person, in their opinion it is permitted to ask a gentile to heal him by means of his sorcery. Likewise, in their opinion it is permitted to ask fortune-tellers, through astrology and the like, whether there is a chance of healing the sick person in a certain way, because the prohibition of inquiring about the future is only because of the positive mitzva of 'You shall be wholehearted', and for the sake of a sick person it is permitted (Terumat Ha-deshen, Pesakim U-khtavim 96; Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 41).

But as halakha in practice, many hold that even for the sake of a sick person it is forbidden to turn to sorcerers or fortune-tellers, because seeking help from sorcerers and diviners is more dangerous than beneficial. As Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote (BY YD 179:16): "And in the book of the Zohar (part 3, 84a) it appears that it is a great prohibition to inquire of sorcerers even for a sick person." And even with demons, for which a few poskim were lenient in using their help, it is not worthwhile to be lenient, for "we have seen that most of those who attach themselves to them do not come out of their hands in peace; therefore one who guards his soul will keep far from them" (Rema and Levush YD 179:16; Ḥokhmat Adam 89:8; see above 26:10). However, when it is a matter of danger to life, there is no prohibition to turn to sorcerers, for pikuaḥ nefesh overrides the prohibitions of the Torah (Maharshal, Responsa 3; Shakh YD 179:1). But in practice it is almost always of no benefit, and it is better to pray to God and to strengthen oneself in the faith that everything God does will be for the good.6
